newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Hashimoto discuss Korea, other issues.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Hashimoto discuss Korea, other issues.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto met on Friday for wide-ranging talks that included possible steps to convince North Korea to join four-nation peace talks.

"The relationship the United States has with Japan is unique and comprehensive and profoundly important to our future and to the stability of the world," Clinton told reporters at the start of the Oval Office talks.
"And we intend to keep working on it and make it better," said Clinton, who met informally at the White House with Hashimoto late on Thursday night.

In response to a question about a cooperation agreement signed earlier this week between China and Russia, Clinton said it posed no threat to the Asia-Pacific region and Hashsimoto called that reply "a splendid answer."

"My view is that the United States should have a partnership ... for stability in the Asian-Pacific region that includes our longstanding alliance with Japan, and a positive relationship with both Russia and with China," Clinton said.

"As long as any agreement they make is consistent with that kind of positive partnership and is not directed in any negative way toward their neighbours, I think ... we don't have anything to worry about."
Hashimoto added: "We are in the transitional period of great change. We are trying to engage, for example, China as a constructive partner in international society."

White House officials, noting that the Japanese leader was spending less than three hours in talks with Clinton, said discussions would not be too detailed on the broad range of issues on their agenda. They included trade and the resurgence of Japan's bilateral trade surplus.

White House officials said, however, that a key aspect of the meeting involved the situation in North Korea and possible additional food-aid to deal with the famine that has generated concerns for political stability in the region.

Although the United States would like Japan to send more food aid, Hashimoto has been cool to the idea. "If North Korea wants humanitarian aid, they should be humane to Japan first," he said on Thursday.
Clinton said he and Hashimoto would have to discuss that topic further.

During negotiations in New York last week, Pyongyang demanded large-scale food aid and other U.S. concessions before it would join proposed four-way peace talks with South Korea, the United States and China.
Washington insists it will not accept conditions from North Korea for its participation in the talks, first proposed by the United States and South Korea a year ago.
At the same time, Washington has been working to relieve the famine conditions in North Korea. It has pledged $25 million in aid, and Seoul has offered $6 million.

Japan, which has provided massive aid in the past, has been upset with Pyongyang because of a big drug seizure aboard a North Korean freighter and allegations that Japanese nationals were allegedly kidnapped by North Korean agents in the late 1970s and 1980s.
Hashimoto was slated to fly to Australia on Saturday and then visit New Zealand through Wednesday before returning to Japan on May 1.
